mcqs.question: Why doesn't doubling a processor's issue width typically double its real-world performance?
options: Because doubling issue width always doubles clock frequency instead of throughput
Because real programs rarely have enough independent, ready instructions every cycle to fill all the extra issue slots
Because superscalar processors are limited to executing only floating-point instructions in parallel
Because compilers refuse to generate code for issue widths greater than 2
mcqs.explanation: Achieved IPC depends on the program actually offering enough independent instructions per cycle; dependence chains, branches, and stalls leave many issue slots empty, so wider issue delivers sharply diminishing returns. It has nothing to do with clock frequency, instruction type restrictions, or compiler limitations.

mcqs.question: Which of these is a genuine structural limiter on how wide a superscalar core can practically go?
options: The number of bits in the program counter
Register-file port count, which must scale with issue width and grows the register file's area and delay disproportionately
The maximum clock frequency achievable by any CMOS process
The number of virtual memory pages the OS can map
mcqs.explanation: Supporting more simultaneous reads/writes per cycle requires more register-file ports, and port count drives area and access-time costs that scale worse than linearly — a real limiter on width. Program-counter width, process-level clock ceilings, and virtual memory paging are unrelated to issue width.

mcqs.question: A narrower superscalar core sometimes outperforms a wider one on the same workload. What best explains this?
options: Wider cores always run at a lower clock frequency by design

Achieved IPC depends on how often the workload actually supplies enough independent, ready instructions to fill issue slots — the narrower core's other strengths (branch prediction, ROB size) can matter more than raw width
Wider cores cannot execute branch instructions at all
Superscalar width only affects power consumption, never performance
mcqs.explanation: Issue width is a ceiling, not a guarantee — if the workload's available ILP or the core's other resources (prediction accuracy, ROB depth) don't support filling extra slots, a narrower but otherwise stronger design can win. The other options are factually wrong generalizations.
